tagline: A desert drive follows the railroad grade past abandoned townsites.
intro: The Transcontinental Railroad Back Country Byway follows the old Central Pacific grade across the flatlands of the Great Salt Lake Desert. The Bureau of Land Management allows three to four hours for the 90-mile drive. Managed as a National Backcountry Byway, it passes ghost towns, foundations, earthworks and culverts that BLM identifies as remnants of the railroad. Expect rough roads in a remote setting.

The grade dates to 1869. Central Pacific had built east from Sacramento while Union Pacific worked west from Omaha, with thousands of workers, mostly of Chinese, Irish or Mormon descent, employed by the two companies. In 1904, Southern Pacific completed the Lucin Cutoff across the Great Salt Lake, bypassing Terrace and reducing its tracks to a little-used branch line. The rails came up in 1942; BLM designated the grade as part of the byway in 1993.

Traveling from the Utah-Nevada border toward the area west of Golden Spike follows the former railroad corridor. At Terrace, a turntable outline survives beside the old railroad bed. Next comes Matlin, with the profile of a rail wye, then Kelton, where abandoned foundations and a cemetery remain. Beyond is Kosmo, with concrete foundations and canals in its western section.

moments.title: Terrace
moments.text: A turntable outline and a pile of red bricks mark Terrace beside the old railroad bed. Established in 1869 as a Central Pacific operations base, the town had a 16-stall roundhouse and an eight-track switchyard. The Lucin Cutoff bypassed it in 1904. The railroad closed its facilities and transferred the division point to Montello, Nevada; many houses and buildings followed. The line was abandoned in 1942, and the surviving cemetery has only three headstones. The town and nearby Terrace Mountain took their names from shoreline terraces left by the former Lake Bonneville in this area.

moments.title: Matlin
moments.text: Matlin survives as the profile of a wye built into the railroad grade in 1900. Chinese railroad workers built the small community and its track-support facilities. Central Pacific Railroad established the town on April 5, 1869. Its recorded population was 15 in 1870 and 25 in 1876, figures that most likely excluded Chinese residents. It depended on the railroad throughout its history and was abandoned when the Lucin Cutoff was finished in 1904. A lightning-caused wildfire in June 2020 damaged or destroyed many artifacts that had remained at the site.

moments.title: Kelton
moments.text: Kelton connected the railroad with a stagecoach route to Boise by the summer of 1869. That route was defunct by July 1884 as other railroads reached northern markets. The Lucin Cutoff later left Kelton on a backup line serving local farmers and ranchers. The 1934 earthquake had already damaged the schoolhouse so severely that it had to be abandoned, though the town itself survived. Even in 1937, it remained a local shipping point with 47 residents. The rails were dismantled in 1942, and the last residents departed, taking some houses with them. Foundations, fallen buildings and a cemetery remain.

practical: Terrace: There are no facilities or services along the byway. BLM advises carrying water and spare tires; flat tires are common. (checked 2026-10-11)
